newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Gold refiners need to add value.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Gold refiners need to add value.

text.p: Australia's largest gold refiner, GoldCorp, said on Wednesday it must provide value-added services if it is to compete in an increasingly overcrowded marketplace.

Margins for simply refining gold have narrowed to the point where the industry sees on average only about 55 Australian cents an ounce of gold, compared with about 80 cents five years ago, Brian Bath, deputy chief executive officer of GoldCorp, and managing director of wholly-owned GoldCorp Australia, said.

GoldCorp refines about 150 tonnes of gold a year from its refineries in Perth and Kalgoorlie, most of which is mined in Australia, although some is shipped in from other countries, including Papua New Guinea and New Zealand.
Its nearest competitor, Johnson Matthey, refines about 100 tonnes in Australia, while Golden West refines about 40 tonnes.
Bath said each of the refineries recognises a need to add value.
"There are no profitable refining opportunities anywhere ... there is no money in refining," Bath said.
In some instances, value is added by producing metal in forms to accommodate foreign markets.
Bath said GoldCorp was also moving toward providing more industrial-type products, such as brazing alloys and wire and sheet.
"Whatever we can do, we will move to the value-added side," he said.
"Refining today has a much broader definition, meaning that the margins are so tight purely through the refining process that you have to get into the value-added process as well."
Moreover, with most gold miners typically electing to take possession of their gold in London rather than Australia, the margin is further diminished, Bath told Reuters in an interview.
"Generally, the refiners would be paying arguably 20 to 25 cents (an ounce) to actually supply them with their gold in London," he said.
"In terms of revenue from refining, we earn less than half of what we earned five years ago," Bath said.
In addition to fees, Australian refiners will retain 0.1 percent of the fine gold to meet losses of gold during processing, Bath said.
It also doesn't pay to get into refining unless you can refine a minimum of between 20 and 30 tonnes of gold a year, Bath said.

However, Australia is not alone in facing competition on refining. In Thailand, where a big market exists for secondary, or remelted, gold to feed a thriving jewellery fabrication industry, a number of refiners are looking for a hold on the market.
"At the moment there are four or five significant players, all apparently getting into the refining business in Thailand," Bath said. "I see it becoming a hopelessly crowded situation."
